notes: Preliminary compromise issue at TCC trial; correspondence and oral evidence on clause 6 are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Agricultural Profiles v PDRL: whether CVA settlement compromise bound parties
key_facts: APL sued PDRL for unpaid roofing supplies while PDRL was subject to a creditors' voluntary arrangement.
The parties negotiated a settlement involving upfront instalments and a balance included in the CVA, but disputed clause 6 fixing a separate payment date for the CVA balance.
APL alleged binding oral agreements on 25 November and 24 December 2004; PDRL treated Mr Dunne's 25 November letter as a counter-offer.
Clause 6, giving APL preferential treatment over other unsecured CVA creditors, remained unresolved through December 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue at the outset of a Technology and Construction Court trial on whether the action had been compromised before substantive adjudication.
enrichment.outcome: The court found no binding compromise; neither the alleged November nor Christmas Eve oral agreement satisfied the requirements for a complete and certain contract, and the action proceeded to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Where a material term remains unresolved—here a collateral CVA payment date giving one creditor an advantage over others—the court will not treat negotiations as a binding compromise; an agreement to agree or insufficiently certain terms cannot bind the parties.
legal_issues: Whether an oral agreement in principle on 25 November 2004 was a binding compromise
Whether a revised oral agreement on 24 December 2004 was binding
Whether clause 6 was an essential or inessential term of the proposed settlement
Application of Foley v Classique Coaches, Walford v Miles and Trentham v Archital Luxfer principles
linked_authorities: Foley v Classique Coaches Ltd [1934] 2 KB 1
Walford v Miles [1992] AC 128
G Percy Trentham Ltd v Archital Luxfer Ltd [1993] 1 Lloyd's Rep 25

confidence.notes: Preliminary compromise ruling and contractual principles are clearly stated, though substantive claims were not tried.

notes: Short contractual construction appeal; Arden LJ's analysis of clause 3.5 and Minimum Royalty is explicit.

enrichment.short_title: CDT v DuPont: construction of minimum royalty shortfall payment dates
key_facts: CDT licensed DuPont to manufacture electroluminescence polymer display technology under a standard-form agreement dated 16 October 2001.
Clause 3.5 required payment of any shortfall between royalties and minimum royalty within 60 days after the first two years and each year thereafter.
Minimum Royalty was defined as US$1 million in relation to each year after 1 January 2003, while Year meant agreement years from the effective date.
CDT contended the parties intended a single US$1 million minimum for the initial two-year period; DuPont argued the natural wording produced later, nil first shortfall calculations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a declaration by Patten J on the true construction of clause 3.5 of a patent licence agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; shortfalls, if any, fall due by 15 December 2004 and on 15 December in each succeeding year on the judge's construction.
enrichment.ratio: A court must give effect to the natural meaning of agreed contractual words and may not rewrite definitions by inserting words or commas to achieve a commercially attractive result unless the agreement or admissible matrix clearly shows a mistake; the words 'if any' qualifying shortfall can cover periods with nil minimum royalty.
legal_issues: Construction of clause 3.5 against the Minimum Royalty definition
Whether the 1 January 2003 date limited the first two-year minimum to US$1 million
Interaction between clause 3.5 and the quarterly payment timetable in clause 3.6
Admissibility of pre-contract negotiations under Investors Compensation Scheme v West Bromwich
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896

confidence.notes: Single issue of construction and unanimous appellate dismissal are clearly recorded.

notes: Ancillary relief appeal on weight of 1999 agreement; judgment applies Edgar, Camm and Smith principles at length.

enrichment.short_title: A v B: upholding 1999 ancillary relief settlement agreement

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

key_facts: The parties separated after a long marriage and entered a written financial agreement in May 1999 giving the husband a £133,000 lump sum, cars, and shares in rugs and an endowment policy.
The district judge found the agreement fair at the time, that the husband was not unduly pressured, and dismissed further ancillary relief claims in 2004.
The husband appealed arguing inadequate disclosure, incomplete legal advice, unfair asset valuation including the Jerusalem flat and Maserati, and changed circumstances by 2004.
Property market rises had left the wife with about 75% of current assets while the husband lived in a larger Georgian house with his new partner.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from a district judge's ancillary relief order enforcing a 1999 separation agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no further lump sum ordered beyond the 1999 agreement, which remained fair and sufficient for the husband's needs.
enrichment.ratio: A prior matrimonial agreement is one ingredient under section 25, not a preliminary determinant; formal agreements fairly arrived at should not be displaced without good and substantial grounds of injustice, but the court must still evaluate all section 25 factors at the hearing date including needs and resources.
legal_issues: Weight to be given to a 1999 separation agreement under Edgar v Edgar
Whether the district judge properly evaluated all section 25 factors in 2004
Treatment of inherited assets and post-separation acquisitions including the Jerusalem flat
Whether non-disclosure of revaluation and imminent inheritance weakened the agreement
linked_authorities: Edgar v Edgar [1980] 1 WLR 1410
Camm v Camm (1983) 4 FLR 577
Smith v Smith [2000] 3 FCR 374
White v White [2001] 1 AC 596

confidence.notes: Detailed asset analysis and appellate disposition are clear though the district judge's brevity on 2004 needs was criticised then cured on appeal.

notes: Long anonymised fact-finding judgment in care proceedings; MSBP/FII label critique and diabetes findings are central.

enrichment.short_title: County Council v mother: fabricated illness findings in split care hearing
key_facts: The local authority applied for care orders in respect of three siblings after concerns about the mother's presentation of illness in the youngest child, Z.
Z had a complex medical history including reported epilepsy, ataxia and developmental delay, culminating in February 2003 hospital admissions.
The mother conceded tampering with urine samples and the court found she fabricated blood sugar readings suggesting diabetes that Z never had.
The eldest boy X returned to the mother's care in November 2004; the younger children remained with their father pending welfare decisions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Split fact-finding hearing in care proceedings to determine threshold facts before a separate welfare hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Detailed findings made on fabricated diabetes evidence and exaggerated illness presentation; threshold submissions reserved; the court cautioned against MSBP/FII labels as substitutes for factual analysis.
enrichment.ratio: Serious child protection findings require cogent evidence judged in full social and medical context, not propensity labels; where a carer fabricates test results risking harmful treatment, that conduct is culpable even if some underlying conditions were genuine and resolving.
legal_issues: Whether the mother fabricated or tampered with medical tests relating to Z's diabetes
Whether Z ever suffered epilepsy and the extent of exaggerated seizure reporting
Admissibility and limits of MSBP and fabricated/induced illness labels
Standard of proof and threshold under section 31 Children Act 1989
linked_authorities: Re H (Minors) (Sexual Abuse: Standard of Proof) [1996] AC 563
Re O and N; Re B (Minors) [2003] 2 WLR 1075
Re U (Serious Injury: Standard of Proof); Re B [2004] 2 FLR 263

confidence.notes: Core findings on diabetes fabrication and judicial caution on diagnostic labels are explicit; final threshold and welfare orders were deferred.

notes: Transport Tribunal statutory appeal; partial remission and recusal issues clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Shamrock Coaches: partial remission and Traffic Commissioner recusal
key_facts: Mrs Jones operated Shamrock Coaches and was found to have breached section 26 by failing without reasonable excuse to run registered local services reliably.
The Transport Tribunal allowed her first appeal in part and remitted limited reconsideration of irregularities and reasonable excuses, but not a full de novo hearing.
Traffic Commissioner Mr Dixon reconvened the inquiry without public advertisement and declined to recuse himself despite criticism of his earlier broad-brush analysis.
The operator refused further submissions at the reconvened hearing, and penalties were largely reaffirmed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Transport Tribunal under section 117(2) and Schedule 4 of the Transport Act 1985.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; partial remission to the same commissioner was lawful, no section 54 advertisement was required for a reconvened limited inquiry, and recusal was not necessary.
enrichment.ratio: The Transport Tribunal may remit for rehearing in whole or in part to the same or a different decision-maker; limited criticism of evidential analysis does not require a fresh commissioner or mandatory re-advertisement where the resumed hearing is a reconvened inquiry on defined issues.
legal_issues: Whether the Transport Tribunal could order partial rather than full remission
Whether the reconvened inquiry required advertisement under section 54
Whether the Traffic Commissioner should have recused himself for apparent bias
Article 6 fair trial implications

confidence.notes: Procedural holdings and dismissal are clearly reasoned on the statutory appeal.

notes: Limitation appeal under section 33; Court of Appeal re-exercises discretion and dismisses claim.

enrichment.short_title: McGhie v BT: section 33 discretion refused for late back injury claim
key_facts: Sean McGhie injured his back pushing cable rods between manholes while working for BT on 26 August 1998.
He issued proceedings in September 2003, more than two years outside the primary three-year limitation period after constructive knowledge was accepted.
The county court judge exercised section 33 discretion in the claimant's favour, emphasising devotion to work and late realisation after proposed 2003 surgery.
The pleaded claim was modest, likely under £20,000, with thin liability particulars and weakened witness evidence due to delay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court preliminary issue decision disapplying the primary limitation period under section 33 Limitation Act 1980.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the court re-exercised section 33 discretion and refused to disapply limitation, dismissing the claim with costs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 33 requires a balance of prejudice with the burden on the claimant; reasonableness alone is insufficient, and proportionality between claim value, costs, evidential prejudice and merits—including liability strength—must be evaluated, following Adams v Bracknell and Robinson v St Helens.
legal_issues: Whether the judge applied the statutory balance of prejudice test under section 33
Whether proportionality between claim size and litigation costs was properly considered
Relevance of the strength of the liability case at the limitation stage
Constructive knowledge under section 14 after Adams v Bracknell Forest
linked_authorities: Adams v Bracknell Forest Borough Council [2004] UKHL 29
Robinson v St Helens Metropolitan Borough Council [2003] PIQR 128
Forbes v Wandsworth Health Authority [1997] QB 402

confidence.notes: Appellate restatement of section 33 principles and re-exercise of discretion are explicit.

notes: Unless order default judgment appeal; Thomas LJ identifies real issues on binding compromise agreement.

enrichment.short_title: CPL v Freeman: default judgment set aside over sand supply settlement
key_facts: CPL contracted with R & L Freeman for sand and gravel supply, paying monthly advances under a written agreement later becoming uneconomic.
At a 29 March 2001 meeting the parties reached a deal to terminate the contract, repay £170,000, deliver free sand, and transfer a Cottam to Ketton haulage contract.
CPL's 30 March letter confirmed key terms but omitted the haulage contract; subsequent drafts never resolved VAT and haulage provisions.
Freeman missed an unless order deadline to serve witness statements by about 30 minutes, and CPL entered default judgment for about £195,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to set aside a default judgment entered after breach of an unless order to serve witness statements.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; default judgment set aside and the action, including counterclaim, to proceed to trial with suggestion of transfer to the Mercantile Court.
enrichment.ratio: On an application to set aside judgment under CPR 3.9, merits are highly material; where there is a real prospect that a businessmen's deal was not binding until reduced to writing and key haulage terms remained disputed, a judge who treated the defence as hopeless misdirected himself.
legal_issues: Whether the 29 March 2001 settlement was immediately binding or subject to formal written variation
Whether haulage contract and VAT terms were ever agreed
Exercise of discretion under CPR 3.9 after slight unless order breach
Whether the counterclaim should also be restored
linked_authorities: Woodhouse v Consignia Plc [2002] EWCA Civ 275
Oberon Investments Ltd v Westbrook Resources Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 710

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on merits and procedural discretion is detailed and conclusive.

notes: Immigration JR on out-of-time appeal extension; N v SSHD Article 3 threshold applied to HIV/leprosy combination.

enrichment.short_title: R (DB) v SSHD: remittal after flawed HIV and leprosy human rights refusal
key_facts: DB, a Ugandan asylum seeker with advanced HIV, leprosy and prior tuberculosis, received specialist treatment in the UK including azathioprine and rifabutin unavailable in Uganda.
An adjudicator rejected his human rights appeal, emphasising general AIDS treatment availability in Uganda and not addressing leprosy.
The IAT refused to extend time for appeal by over five months without adequate reasons on medical evidence.
Expert evidence indicated withdrawal of treatment in Uganda would cause rapid deterioration, disfigurement, blindness risk and social ostracism.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal to extend time for an out-of-time human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: IAT decision quashed and remitted for fresh consideration; the Article 3 claim was at least arguable under N v SSHD despite significant delay.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator ignores a significant aspect of a claimant's medical condition and the IAT fails to grapple with arguable Article 3 material under the strict N test, Wednesbury review requires remittal; delay without satisfactory explanation remains a weighty factor but does not automatically preclude extension where errors are material.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred by failing to consider leprosy in the Article 3 assessment
Application of N v Secretary of State for the Home Department to combined HIV and leprosy
Whether special circumstances justified extending time under rule 16 Immigration and Asylum Procedure Rules 2003
Availability of rifabutin and azathioprine treatment in Uganda
linked_authorities: N v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 1369
D v United Kingdom (1997) 24 EHRR 423
Tofik v Immigration Appeal Tribunal [2003] EWCA Civ 1138

confidence.notes: Quashing order, identified adjudicator errors and remittal terms are clearly set out.

notes: Unusual summary costs application against solicitors; Colman J refuses for disputed authority and loss proof.

enrichment.short_title: Houlder v Jackson Parton: summary warranty of authority costs refused
key_facts: Skylight Maritime, a Panamanian one-yacht company, claimed total loss of TIGER II through solicitors Jackson Parton against insurers and later joined placing brokers Houlder.
JP relied on instructions from broker Inship and George Sigalas, but corporate documentation and Panamanian board authority were missing after Sigalas's death.
Langley J struck out the claim when JP came off the record; Houlder then sought summary indemnity costs against JP for unauthorised litigation.
Skylight appeared to have no assets apart from the disputed insurance claim, complicating proof of recoverable loss.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court summary application for indemnity costs against solicitors for allegedly commencing and continuing proceedings without client authority.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; Houlder must bring separate proceedings for breach of warranty of authority because authority, scope and loss issues require full trial.
enrichment.ratio: The court's summary jurisdiction over solicitors acting without authority is compensatory and should not be used where authority from a foreign corporate client, scope of retainer to sue brokers, and measurable loss are genuinely disputed; an insolvent or assetless apparent client limits recoverable damages even if authority existed.
legal_issues: Whether Jackson Parton had authority from Skylight to commence and continue proceedings
Whether Panamanian law required board resolutions beyond Sigalas's shareholder status
Whether authority to sue insurers extended to joining Houlder after Sigalas's death
Appropriate measure of loss where the apparent client had no assets
linked_authorities: Yonge v Toynbee [1910] 1 KB 215
Collen v Wright (1857) 8 E&B 647
Habton Farms Ltd v Nimmo [2004] QB 1

confidence.notes: Interlocutory refusal and reasoning on disputed facts and loss are explicit; underlying claim merits undetermined.

notes: CPO challenge to Arsenal Ashburton Grove scheme; Secretary of State disagreement with Inspector upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Alliance Spring v SSHD: Arsenal stadium CPO confirmation upheld
key_facts: Arsenal FC proposed relocating from Highbury to a 60,000-seat stadium at Ashburton Grove with linked regeneration at Lough Road and the former Highbury site.
Islington Council granted planning permission in May 2002 and made a compulsory purchase order covering 134 plots including Queensland Road businesses.
The Inspector recommended against confirmation, criticising opportunistic regeneration justification and willingness to proceed with the stadium without the CPO.
The Secretary of State disagreed, finding a compelling public interest in comprehensive regeneration and confirmed the order with modifications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court challenge under section 23 Acquisition of Land Act 1981 to confirmation of a compulsory purchase order for the Ashburton Grove scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Secretary of State lawfully concluded there was a compelling case in the public interest and proportionate interference with property rights.
enrichment.ratio: On CPO confirmation the Secretary of State may properly differ from an inspector on evaluative judgments where planning permission already exists; a stadium-led private development can still constitute a comprehensive regeneration scheme under section 226(4) even if the council does not itself undertake the works.
legal_issues: Whether the main purpose of the CPO was AFC's stadium or comprehensive regeneration
Whether a compelling public interest justified compulsory acquisition under Circular 02/03
Proportionality under Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR for Queensland Road businesses
Whether the Secretary of State could disagree with the Inspector without reopening the inquiry
linked_authorities: R (Ghadami) v Harlow District Council [2002] EWHC 2044 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Final dismissal and key public-law conclusions on purpose and proportionality are clearly expressed.
